requested.title: Self-hosted LLM relay follows attacker-controlled redirects to private services

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: A regular authenticated user can save a `generic` BYOK base URL through `app/api/account/ai-keys/route.ts`; it initially calls `assertPublicHttpUrl`, and `getUserByok` repeats that validation before a server-side agent run. `assertPublicHttpUrl` correctly rejects private resolutions at validation time, but it only returns an address for callers that use the pinned-request path; neither the relay configuration nor the runner retains or uses that address. `executeAgentRun` passes the resolved user-controlled `baseUrl` to `SelfHostedSandbox.configureLlmRelay`, which sends it over the trusted runner API, and the runner's `completionUrl` only checks URL syntax and HTTP(S). On each completion, `deploy/self-hosted/agent-runner.mjs` performs plain `fetch(relay.url, { method: "POST", ... })`, whose default redirect mode follows redirects and whose DNS connection is not pinned. Thus, an attacker-controlled publicly resolvable provider can issue a 307/308 redirect from its `/chat/completions` endpoint to a private hostname or address reachable from the runner, causing the privileged runner to make the request; DNS can likewise change after the application's preliminary lookup. This is meaningful in the supplied Compose profiles because the runner is attached to the internal `private` network as well as egress and has the Docker socket mounted, while the isolated sandbox itself only receives the egress network. Authentication and the per-run relay control token restrict who can configure and invoke a relay, but do not prevent a legitimate low-privilege user from configuring their own generic provider and starting their own agent run. Git history shows the vulnerable relay and plain fetch were introduced together in commit `18465f29`; no subsequent change replaces it with `safeFetch`, disables redirects, or validates and pins every hop.
